This document describes how the platform's informal digital lending product extends short-term credit to individual borrowers through a mobile application, without the branch network, group guarantee structure, or formal underwriting committee used elsewhere in the business. Loans are approved automatically by a scoring model that evaluates a borrower's mobile money transaction history, airtime top-up frequency, and repayment behavior on any prior loans taken through the same application, producing a decision within a few seconds of a borrower submitting a request.

Borrowers who have never taken a loan through the platform before are limited to a small first loan, typically enough to cover an emergency expense, disbursed directly into their mobile money wallet the moment the automated decision comes back positive. Repayment is expected within thirty days, and the borrower can repay early at any point without penalty, though a late repayment past the due date accrues a daily fee that continues to accumulate until the balance is cleared or the loan is written off entirely.

As a borrower repays several loans on time, the scoring model gradually increases both the loan size it is willing to offer and the repayment window it allows, moving from the initial thirty-day term toward periods as long as ninety days for borrowers who have built a long history of on-time repayment. Borrowers who miss a repayment deadline are automatically restricted from taking a new loan until the overdue balance is settled, and a pattern of repeated late payment permanently lowers the maximum loan size the model will ever offer that borrower again, regardless of how much time passes afterward.

Because there is no branch network and no loan officer assigned to any individual borrower, collections on an overdue balance happen entirely through automated reminders sent by text message and push notification, escalating in frequency and tone as a balance ages further past its due date. A balance that remains unpaid for more than ninety days is referred to a third-party collections agency under a separate agreement, and the borrower's record is flagged in the platform's shared credit bureau feed, which several other digital lenders in the same market also consult before approving their own loans.

The platform does not currently offer any restructuring or hardship program for borrowers experiencing genuine financial difficulty, a gap that has drawn criticism from consumer advocates who argue that automated, high-frequency lending of this kind can trap borrowers in a cycle of repeated small loans taken out primarily to cover the fees and penalties from a previous one. Management has acknowledged the criticism in internal discussions but has not yet committed to a specific timeline for introducing any formal hardship accommodation, citing the operational complexity of retrofitting a manual review process onto a lending flow that was designed from the outset to require no human intervention at any stage of the loan lifecycle.

Regulatory oversight of this particular lending channel remains limited compared to the bank's formal commercial and SACCO lending lines described elsewhere in this policy set, since the applicable digital lending regulations in most of the jurisdictions where the platform operates were only recently introduced and are still being interpreted by both regulators and industry participants, leaving considerable ambiguity about exactly which disclosure and interest-rate-cap requirements ultimately apply to a fully automated, app-based lending product of this kind.
